title: How to Make Friends as an Adult: A Practical, Honest Guide
h1: How to Make Friends as an Adult: A Practical, Honest Guide
description: Learn how to make friends as an adult with practical steps: where to meet people, how to turn acquaintances into friends, and how to keep friendships going.
keyword: how to make friends as an adult
excerpt: Making friends gets harder after school, but it's far from impossible. Where to meet people, how to follow up, and how to keep friendships alive.
intro:
As a kid, friendship mostly happened to you. You sat next to someone in class, played on the same team, or lived on the same street, and before long you were inseparable. As an adult, those built-in structures fade. Work, family, moves and busy schedules make it easy to look up one day and realize your circle has shrunk.

If that's where you are, you're far from alone, and nothing is wrong with you. Making friends as an adult simply takes more intention. This guide covers where to meet people, how to turn a friendly acquaintance into an actual friend, and how to keep friendships going once you have them, with extra tips if you're shy.
body:
Why making friends feels harder as an adult

Friendships tend to grow from three ingredients: repeated contact, time that isn't rushed, and settings where people feel comfortable opening up. School and college offer all three by default. Adult life often offers none. You might see coworkers every day, but conversations stay professional. You might meet great people at a party, but never see them again.

Understanding this helps in two ways. First, it takes the shame out of feeling lonely, because it's a structural problem, not a personal failing. Second, it points to the solution: deliberately put yourself in situations that recreate those three ingredients.

Tip: Choose activities that meet regularly, like a weekly class or monthly club, over one-off events. Seeing the same faces again and again is what turns strangers into friends.

Join a club, class or organization

Shared interests are the easiest starting point for friendship because they give you something to talk about from the start. Look for groups that meet on a regular schedule:

  • Hobby clubs: book clubs, board game nights, running or cycling groups, hiking meetups, knitting circles.
  • Classes: pottery, cooking, dance, language, improv or martial arts.
  • Recreational sports leagues: kickball, volleyball, softball and pickleball leagues often welcome beginners.
  • Faith or community organizations: congregations, cultural associations and neighborhood groups.
  • Professional groups: industry meetups or alumni associations, which can lead to friendships outside work.

Commit to showing up several times before deciding whether a group is right for you. The first meeting is almost always awkward. By the third or fourth, people start recognizing you, and conversations get easier.

Use social apps and online communities wisely

Technology can be a great on-ramp to in-person friendships. Many people use friendship-focused apps, neighborhood forums and local social media groups to find others with similar interests or life stages, such as new parents, recent transplants or remote workers.

A few tips to make online connections work:

  • Be specific in your profile about what you enjoy and what kind of friendship you're looking for.
  • Move from messaging to meeting fairly quickly, choosing a public place for a first meetup.
  • Suggest an activity rather than just 'hanging out,' like a coffee walk, a trivia night or a farmers market.
  • Don't take it personally if some conversations fizzle. That happens to everyone.

Online interest groups centered on a hobby or a city can also lead to local meetups. If you've recently moved, our guide on how to meet new people has more ideas.

Volunteer for something you care about

Volunteering is one of the most underrated ways to make friends. You work side by side toward a shared goal, which naturally creates conversation and camaraderie. You also meet people who care about the same causes you do, which is a strong foundation for friendship.

Look for recurring roles, like a weekly shift at a food bank, an animal shelter, a literacy program or a community garden. Regular commitments give you repeat contact with the same people, and the work itself takes the pressure off making conversation.

Turn acquaintances into friends

Most adults have plenty of acquaintances: friendly coworkers, neighbors, people from the gym. The missing step is usually the invitation. Someone has to suggest spending time together outside the usual setting, and it can be you.

How to make the first move

  • Make it specific. 'We should hang out sometime' rarely happens. 'Want to grab tacos after the meetup on Thursday?' usually does.
  • Tie it to a shared interest. 'I'm going to that photography exhibit Saturday. Want to come?'
  • Keep the first plan short and low-key. Coffee, a walk or a quick lunch is less of a commitment than a whole evening.
  • Follow up. If it went well, suggest a second plan within a week or two. Momentum matters.

It's normal to feel a little vulnerable doing this. Most people are pleased to be invited, even if they can't make it, because many of them are hoping someone else will reach out first.

Tip: If someone says no once, try one more time with a different plan. If they decline twice without suggesting an alternative, it's okay to let them come to you.

Maintain a realistic attitude

Adult friendships often take longer to form than you'd expect. Deep friendships typically require many hours of shared time, and you won't click with everyone you meet. Some people will be activity friends, some will become close confidants, and some will drift away. All of that is normal.

A few expectations that help:

  • Quality grows slowly. Don't judge a potential friendship by the first conversation.
  • Not every invitation will be returned. People are busy; it's rarely personal.
  • You may need to initiate more than you'd like. That's okay, especially at first.
  • A few close friends are plenty. You don't need a huge circle to feel connected.

Value and nurture the friends you have

Making new friends is important, but so is caring for existing ones. Friendships need maintenance, just like romantic relationships. Reach out to old friends you've lost touch with. A simple 'I was thinking about you, how are you?' can reignite a connection.

Ways to keep friendships strong:

  • Check in regularly, even with a short text or voice note.
  • Remember birthdays and important events.
  • Show up when they need support, not just when it's convenient.
  • Celebrate their wins genuinely.
  • Create rituals, like a monthly dinner, a weekly call or an annual trip.

Friendship skills overlap a lot with relationship skills. Our article on how to cheer someone up is a great resource for being a supportive friend.

Step away from screens, at least sometimes

Phones and streaming are comfortable, and after a long day it's tempting to stay in every night. But screens can quietly replace the effort friendship requires. Scrolling through friends' updates can feel like staying in touch without actually connecting.

Try small changes: leave your phone in your pocket at a coffee shop and chat with the person next to you, say yes to one invitation a week, or replace a night of scrolling with a call to a friend. Real-life interaction builds the kind of closeness that likes and comments can't.

If you're shy or socially anxious

Shyness can make every step feel harder, but it doesn't have to stop you. Many shy people make wonderful, loyal friends. A few strategies to ease in:

  • Start with structured activities. Classes and volunteering have built-in tasks, so there's less pressure to fill silence.
  • Prepare a few questions. 'How did you get into this?' and 'What else do you like to do around here?' work almost anywhere.
  • Bring a friend at first. Having a familiar face can make new situations less daunting.
  • Celebrate small wins. Saying hi to someone new counts.

If loneliness or anxiety feels heavy or persistent, talking with a licensed therapist can be a real help. Our guides on how to deal with loneliness and how to be happy with yourself also offer practical support.

The bottom line

Learning how to make friends as an adult comes down to intention and repetition. Choose activities that meet regularly, be the person who extends specific invitations, keep realistic expectations and nurture the friendships you already have. It takes time, but every small step, a new class, a follow-up text, a coffee invitation, builds toward a circle of people who know and care about you. Explore more in our relationships section.
takeaways: Adult friendships need repeated contact, unhurried time and comfortable settings.
Join groups that meet regularly and keep showing up past the awkward first visit.
Turn acquaintances into friends with specific, low-key invitations.
Expect friendships to take time, and don't take busy schedules personally.
Maintain existing friendships with regular check-ins and shared rituals.

faq.q: Why is it so hard to make friends as an adult?
faq.a: Adult life removes many of the natural structures that built friendships earlier, like daily classes, shared dorms and free time. Work, family and moving also limit opportunities. The fix is to recreate repeated, relaxed contact through clubs, classes, volunteering and regular invitations rather than waiting for friendships to happen on their own.

faq.q: Where is the best place to make friends as an adult?
faq.a: Places with recurring activities work best: hobby clubs, classes, recreational sports leagues, volunteer roles and community or faith groups. Seeing the same people regularly gives friendships time to grow. Friendship apps and local online groups can also help you find people with similar interests, especially after a move.

faq.q: How do you turn an acquaintance into a friend?
faq.a: Make a specific, low-pressure invitation, such as coffee after an event you both attend or a walk on the weekend. Keep the first plan short, then follow up with another plan if it went well. Consistent contact and showing genuine interest in their life gradually deepen the connection.

faq.q: Is it normal to have no friends as an adult?
faq.a: It's more common than many people realize, especially after moves, breakups, new jobs or becoming a parent. It doesn't mean something is wrong with you. Taking small, regular steps to meet people usually helps. If loneliness feels overwhelming, consider talking with a licensed therapist for extra support.
